name: Jammu & Kashmir
intro: Jammu and Kashmir is the one state in this archive the 2008 delimitation never touched. Its assembly seats were drawn under the state's own constitution and Representation of the People Act, last by the Gupta Commission in 1995 on the 1981 census, and in 2002 the state froze any further redrawing until 2026. The freeze ended with the state itself: after Article 370 was read down in 2019 and the state was reorganised, a fresh Delimitation Commission redrew the constituencies in 2022, and the new map was first contested in 2024.

map_caveats: This is the only state in the archive whose two maps are not the 1976 and 2008 delimitation orders. The 2008 order did not extend to Jammu and Kashmir, whose assembly constituencies were drawn under the state's own law until 2019. The comparison here is between the 1995 order as amended in 2019 and the 2022 order of the Delimitation Commission.

The pre-2022 map is shown with 83 seats. The 1995 order provided 87, of which four were in Ladakh: Nubra, Leh, Kargil and Zanskar. Ladakh became a separate union territory in 2019 and those seats ceased to form part of the Jammu and Kashmir assembly. They have been removed here so that the two maps cover the same ground, but no election was ever held on an 83-seat map: all four elections shown on this side, from 1996 to 2014, were contested across 87 seats. Seat numbers on the pre-2022 side are those used at those elections, which is why they run to 87 with four numbers absent.

Territory lineage is given for all seats in both orders, on two footings, and each seat record states which applies to it. For 73 of the 83 pre-2022 seats the link is derived from the text of the 2019 schedule and the 2022 order, which describe constituencies in the same vocabulary of tehsils and patwar circles. For the remaining ten the successor shown is the one holding the largest share of the old seat's area, inferred from the boundaries alone.

The two mapped layers come from different sources and have not been adjusted to fit one another. Their outlines agree to an intersection-over-union of 0.92, and testing showed no translation or scaling that improved on that, so the difference is taken to be digitisation rather than misregistration.

Reservation status is taken from the statutory text rather than from the constituency geometry, whose reservation field is empty for both layers. The 2019 schedule marks seven Scheduled Caste seats on the pre-2022 map; the 2022 order provides seven Scheduled Caste and nine Scheduled Tribe seats, the first time tribal seats have been reserved in the territory.
Territory percentages are measured from the mapped boundaries in every case, and are areal shares, not shares of the electorate.

Both maps cover only the territory under Indian administration, as the source digitisations do. Areas claimed but not administered are not shown, and no view is expressed here on the status of any boundary.

Both maps are grouped by the twenty districts of the 2022 order. The pre-2022 digitisation carried no district field, only parliamentary constituencies, so each pre-2022 seat is grouped by the district its territory mostly falls within.
footnotes: The 1995 order was made by a commission under Justice K. K. Gupta while the state was under President's rule, using the 1981 census; no census was held in Jammu and Kashmir in 1991.
The 2022 order added seven seats, six in the Jammu division and one in the Kashmir division, taking the assembly from 83 effective seats to 90.
Reservation status reflects the category in force at the time of the relevant order, not any later reclassification.
